couplets.gloss: Walk away from anything that would degrade you, even something you feel you cannot live without.
couplets.sensitive: puts honour above staying alive

edges.reason: Says to drop whatever would lower you, even what you can’t do without.
edges.quote: give them up if they would lower you

couplets.gloss: People who want to be remembered well won't do anything shameful, even when it would make them famous.

edges.reason: Those who care for their name refuse wrong even when wrong would bring them glory.
edges.quote: won’t do anything unworthy, even for glory

edges.reason: For someone asked to stoop in order to rise: a name worth keeping is not traded for advancement.
edges.quote: won’t do anything unworthy

couplets.gloss: Stay humble while things go well, and keep your head up when they go badly.

edges.reason: Asks for bending low at exactly the moment you have the most.
edges.quote: In plenty, bow low

edges.reason: When your means shrink, that is the time to stand straightest.
edges.quote: When your means shrink, stand tall

edges.reason: A plain instruction to anyone riding high: plenty is the time to bow.
edges.quote: In plenty, bow low

couplets.gloss: People who fall from their good standing become like hair cut off the head: once part of you, now swept out as rubbish.
couplets.sensitive: calls the disgraced discarded refuse

edges.reason: Shows the price of losing your standing: to be like hair that has dropped from the head.
edges.quote: like hair fallen from the head

couplets.gloss: Even the most towering figures shrink if they do one mean thing, however tiny it is.

edges.reason: A lapse no bigger than a crab’s-eye seed is enough to bring such a person down.
edges.quote: will still fall if they do something low

edges.reason: Measures a person’s stature as a hill, then sets a tiny seed against it.
edges.quote: as high as a hill

couplets.gloss: It wins you no fame and no heaven, so why make a living by trailing after people who look down on you?

edges.reason: Asks what trailing after those who despise you could ever gain, since it brings neither fame nor the land of the gods.
edges.quote: why follow behind those who despise you?

edges.reason: Puts the question straight to someone staying close to those who scorn them: what does it win you?
edges.quote: why follow behind those who despise you?

couplets.gloss: Better to be counted as finished on the spot than to get by clinging to people who hold you in contempt.
couplets.sensitive: prefers death to living under scorn

edges.reason: Ranks living off the people who scorn you as worse than ruin itself.
edges.quote: to live by trailing after those who spurn you

couplets.gloss: Is the body going to last forever, that people protect it even when the price is their honour?
couplets.sensitive: scorns staying alive at the cost of honour

edges.reason: Mocks saving your flesh at the cost of your dignity by asking whether that is any medicine.
edges.quote: is a life of tending your flesh any medicine?

couplets.gloss: Like the yak said to die once it loses its hair, some people cannot go on after they lose their honour.
couplets.sensitive: presents ending one's life as the answer to lost honour

edges.reason: Likens those who cannot bear lost honour to the yak that won’t live without its hair.
edges.quote: Like the yak that won’t live if it loses its hair

couplets.gloss: The whole world bows in admiration to people so honourable that they will not go on living in disgrace.
couplets.sensitive: praises refusing to outlive disgrace

edges.reason: Has the whole world joining its hands before those who put their name above their life.
edges.quote: The world bows down and praises the radiance

couplets.gloss: Greatness is the drive to do something worthy; smallness is telling yourself you can get by without it.

edges.reason: Makes a wealth of spirit the light a person has, which is what this chapter calls greatness.
edges.quote: A person’s light is a wealth of spirit

edges.reason: Names disgrace as a single thought: that you can live without such spirit.
edges.quote: A person’s disgrace is to say, “I can live without that.”

edges.reason: Makes a wealth of spirit the very thing that gives a person their light.
edges.quote: a wealth of spirit

couplets.gloss: Everyone comes into the world the same way; what separates people is the life they go on to live.

edges.reason: Birth makes no difference between living beings. What each one does decides their distinction.
edges.quote: because what they do is different

couplets.gloss: High rank doesn't make a mean person high, and low rank doesn't make a fine person low.

edges.reason: Takes rank out of the test: high and low are settled by what one is, not where one stands.
edges.quote: even if they are lowborn, those that are not low are not low

couplets.gloss: Like a faithful woman's fidelity, greatness lasts only if you hold yourself to it from within.

edges.reason: Gives its one condition: greatness is there only if you guard yourself.
edges.quote: greatness too comes only if you guard yourself

edges.reason: Holds up women of undivided heart, who guard themselves, as the model for keeping greatness.
edges.quote: women of undivided heart

couplets.gloss: Truly great people know how to go about things and pull off what others can't.

edges.reason: Marks the great by the hard deeds they can finish, by the right means.
edges.quote: The great will carry out hard deeds

couplets.gloss: Small-minded people simply never think of respecting great people and earning their goodwill.

edges.reason: Says respect for those above them is simply not in small natures.
edges.quote: It never enters the minds of the small

couplets.gloss: When good fortune lands on small-minded people, their arrogance goes completely out of control.

edges.reason: Distinction in unworthy hands turns to nothing but excess.
edges.quote: when it falls to the unworthy, turns to nothing but excess

couplets.gloss: Really great people stay humble; small people boast about themselves to everyone.

edges.reason: Greatness never puts itself forward, and that is how it is known.
edges.quote: Greatness always bends low

edges.reason: Smallness has to admire itself and dress itself up.
edges.quote: Smallness admires itself and dresses itself up

couplets.gloss: A great person has no airs and is gracious to everyone; a small person rides high on pride and insolence.

edges.reason: Measures greatness by having no pride at all.
edges.quote: Greatness is having no pride

edges.reason: Shows smallness riding on pride, all the way to its limit.
edges.quote: Smallness is riding on pride, all the way to its limit

couplets.gloss: Great people cover for others' weaknesses; small people talk about nothing but other people's faults.

edges.reason: The great keep other people's failings out of sight.
edges.quote: Greatness hides another’s shame

edges.reason: Smallness has only faults to talk about.
edges.quote: Smallness speaks of nothing but faults

couplets.gloss: People set on building real character treat every good act as simply their duty.

edges.reason: Once someone takes up worth, every good thing becomes a duty.
edges.quote: every good thing is a duty

couplets.gloss: What makes good people beautiful is their character; physical looks add nothing to it.

edges.reason: Finds the only real goodness of the worthy in their character and none anywhere else.
edges.quote: The goodness of the worthy is goodness of character

couplets.gloss: Five things hold up a good character: love, a sense of shame, helpfulness, tolerance of others' failings and honesty.

edges.reason: Names the five pillars that hold up worth.
edges.quote: the five pillars that hold up worth

edges.reason: First of the five is loving-kindness.
edges.quote: Loving-kindness

edges.reason: Second comes being able to feel shame.
edges.quote: a sense of shame

edges.reason: Helpfulness, the readiness to be of use, stands third.
edges.quote: helpfulness

edges.reason: Fourth is considerateness, the kindly eye towards other people.
edges.quote: considerateness

edges.reason: Truthfulness closes the list as the fifth pillar.
edges.quote: truthfulness

couplets.gloss: A holy person's goodness lies in not killing; a person of character's goodness lies in not speaking of others' faults.

edges.reason: Makes not speaking of others’ wrongs the mark of worth, as not killing marks penance.
edges.quote: The good of worth lies in not speaking of others’ wrongs

edges.reason: Others’ wrongs are the one thing a person of worth above all won’t talk about.
edges.quote: not speaking of others’ wrongs

edges.reason: Gives penance a single defining good, that of not killing.
edges.quote: The good of penance lies in not killing

couplets.gloss: Real power shows itself in being humble, and humility is also how a good person holds off opponents.

edges.reason: Turns the usual idea round: bowing is what strength consists of, and a weapon against enemies.
edges.quote: The strength of the capable is bowing

couplets.gloss: The real test of character is admitting someone is better than you, even someone you rank beneath you.

edges.reason: Sets the test: accepting defeat even from those who are not your equals.
edges.quote: Accepting defeat, even from those who are not your equals

edges.reason: Asks for the stone on which worth can be rubbed and proved, like gold.
edges.quote: What is the touchstone of worth?

couplets.gloss: What is your goodness worth if you won't do good even to the people who hurt you?
couplets.sensitive: urges doing good to those who harm you

edges.reason: Expects good to be returned for injury, not merely injury to be withheld.
edges.quote: do kindness even to those who have done you harm

edges.reason: Asks what use worth has if kindness stops at those who hurt you.
edges.quote: What use is worth

couplets.gloss: Being poor is no shame for someone who has the solid strength of good character.

edges.reason: The strength of worth is enough to lift the shame from having nothing.
edges.quote: if you have the strength called worth

edges.reason: Calls character the riches a man with empty pockets can still own.
edges.quote: the wealth that is called character

edges.reason: Tells someone ashamed of having little that the lack itself is no disgrace.
edges.quote: Having nothing is no disgrace

couplets.gloss: People who won't stray from what's right even if the whole world turns upside down are the anchor of good character.

edges.reason: Those called the ocean of worth hold firm even when the age itself shifts.
edges.quote: those called the ocean of worth will not shift

couplets.gloss: If good people ever gave up their goodness, even the earth couldn't carry the weight of humanity.

edges.reason: Makes the worth of the worthy what the earth’s bearing of its load depends on.
edges.quote: If the worthy fall from their worth

edges.reason: Pictures the earth as a carrier who could not take the load without the worthy.
edges.quote: even the great earth can’t bear its load

couplets.gloss: They say good manners come easily to people who are approachable and welcome everyone.

edges.reason: Traces courtesy to an open welcome given to all comers.
edges.quote: being easy to approach, for anyone at all

couplets.gloss: True courtesy comes from two things together: a loving nature and a good family upbringing.

edges.reason: States what courtesy is made of: exactly two things together.
edges.quote: these two are the way of courtesy

edges.reason: Loving-kindness is the first of the two.
edges.quote: Having loving-kindness

edges.reason: Birth in a good family is the second.
edges.quote: being born into a good family

couplets.gloss: People aren't really alike because their bodies look alike; the likeness that counts is in how they behave.

edges.reason: Refuses the body as the measure of a person: courtesy is the only true likeness.
edges.quote: True likeness is likeness in the courtesy that draws people close

couplets.gloss: The world values the manners of people who are fair, decent and useful to others.

edges.reason: The world prizes the bearing of those who are just and of use to others.
edges.quote: The world praises the courtesy

couplets.gloss: Put-downs hurt even as a joke, so well-mannered people stay polite even to their enemies.

edges.reason: Those who know what others feel stay courteous even towards an enemy.
edges.quote: stay courteous, even in enmity

edges.reason: A sneer wounds even when it is only meant as a joke.
edges.quote: Scorn hurts, even in fun

couplets.gloss: The world keeps running because of decent, well-mannered people; without them all harmony would be gone.

edges.reason: Credits the courteous with keeping the world going at all.
edges.quote: The world goes on because of the courteous

couplets.gloss: However keen their minds, people without basic human decency are just blocks of timber.

edges.reason: Sharp wits count for nothing once human courtesy is missing.
edges.quote: Those without human courtesy

edges.reason: Gives clever people the keen edge of a file, an edge with nothing human behind it.
edges.quote: as sharp as a file

edges.reason: Makes those without courtesy trees: dull timber set against the file’s bite.
edges.quote: are like trees

couplets.gloss: Being rude is a low thing to do, even to people who act coldly and treat you unfairly.
couplets.sensitive: asks courtesy towards those who mistreat you

edges.reason: Holds that discourtesy lowers you even when the other person has been unkind.
edges.quote: it is low to fail in courtesy

couplets.gloss: For people who can't laugh or be cheerful, the whole vast world is dark even in broad daylight.
couplets.sensitive: can read as condemning the depressed

edges.reason: To those who can’t laugh the whole world lies in darkness, though it is day.
edges.quote: lies in darkness, even by day

couplets.gloss: A big fortune owned by an ungracious person goes bad, like good milk spoiled by a dirty pot.

edges.reason: Someone without courtesy spoils great wealth the way a bad pot spoils good milk.
edges.quote: like good milk gone sour from a bad pot

couplets.gloss: Someone who piles up riches at home and never touches them has, in effect, already died.

edges.reason: Riches neither spent nor enjoyed do their owner no more good than a corpse.
edges.quote: stores up great heaps of wealth and doesn’t eat from it

edges.reason: Pronounces the unspending rich man dead while he still breathes.
edges.quote: He is a dead man

edges.reason: Speaks to anyone with a full store and no use of it: the unused pile gives no life.
edges.quote: there is nothing he can do with it

couplets.gloss: A person who thinks money is everything and hoards it without giving will be reborn as something wretched.

edges.reason: Promises a wretched birth to anyone who takes wealth for everything and gives nothing.
edges.quote: That delusion brings a wretched birth

couplets.gloss: People who only care about piling up money and have no wish to be well thought of just weigh down the earth.

edges.reason: Sees nothing in a life of pure accumulation, with no care for a good name, but dead weight.
edges.quote: crave piling up wealth and don’t want fame

edges.reason: The earth has to carry such people, and they are only a load on her.
edges.quote: only a load on the earth

couplets.gloss: If nobody has any fondness for you, what exactly do you think you will leave behind when you die?

edges.reason: A man nobody cares for leaves nothing behind, so being remembered is the only thing that outlasts him.
edges.quote: What does he think he will leave behind

couplets.gloss: People who neither share their money nor spend it on themselves have nothing, even with millions in the bank.

edges.reason: Whoever neither gives nor enjoys has nothing, however high the heap.
edges.quote: have nothing, even with ten million heaped on ten million

edges.reason: Names the trap exactly: money you won't share or enjoy is money you do not have.
edges.quote: neither give nor enjoy have nothing

couplets.gloss: A person who neither enjoys his wealth nor gives to those who deserve it is a sickness in a great fortune.

edges.reason: Such an owner harms the wealth he holds, neither tasting it nor sharing it.
edges.quote: won’t enjoy it himself and has no habit of giving to the deserving

edges.reason: Makes the man himself an illness that great wealth has caught.
edges.quote: a sickness to great wealth

couplets.gloss: Money held by someone who gives nothing to the needy is like a beautiful woman growing old alone: a waste.

edges.reason: Wealth that never reaches the needy withers unused, as beauty does when it grows old alone.
edges.quote: gives nothing to those who have nothing

couplets.sensitive: likens a woman who ages unmarried to wasted wealth

couplets.gloss: The wealth of someone nobody likes is like a poison tree fruiting in the middle of town: there, but no use to anyone.

edges.reason: Plants a poison tree where the village's fruit tree should stand: ripe, central and useless.
edges.quote: a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of the village

couplets.gloss: Money piled up by shutting out love, ignoring what's right and going without yourself only ends up with strangers.

edges.reason: Punishing yourself and ignoring loving-kindness and righteousness only gathers wealth for others to take.
edges.quote: to gather bright wealth, and others take it

couplets.gloss: When a generous rich person runs short after giving so much, it passes quickly, like a cloud that has rained itself out.

edges.reason: Sets the rich of good name beside the rain cloud, the great giver, whose shortage doesn’t last.
edges.quote: A short spell of hardship for the wealthy of good name

edges.reason: A person of good name run dry is only a rain cloud that will fill again.
edges.quote: like a rain cloud running dry

couplets.gloss: Good people feel shame about wrong actions, which is a very different thing from a pretty girl's shy blush.

edges.reason: Separates real shame, felt at an act, from the shyness of women.
edges.quote: Real shame is shrinking from an act

couplets.gloss: Everyone shares food, clothing and children; what really sets people apart is a sense of shame.

edges.reason: Food, clothing and the rest are common to all. A sense of shame alone marks a person out.
edges.quote: What marks out a person is a sense of shame

couplets.gloss: As all life is lodged in a body, goodness of character is lodged in the sense of shame.

edges.reason: Worth is bound to shame, as life is to flesh.
edges.quote: Worth is bound to the good called shame

edges.reason: Life lodged in the body gives the pattern for worth lodged in shame.
edges.quote: All life is bound to flesh

couplets.gloss: A sense of shame is what really adorns good people; without it, a person's proud strut is painful to watch.

edges.reason: Without shame, a proud walk is only a disease.
edges.quote: Without it, isn’t a proud walk a disease?

edges.reason: Hangs shame on the worthy as their ornament.
edges.quote: shame the ornament of the worthy

couplets.gloss: People who feel as ashamed of others' disgrace as of their own are, the world says, where shame truly lives.

edges.reason: Praises those who feel the same shame at another’s blame as at their own.
edges.quote: ashamed of others’ blame as well as their own

couplets.gloss: The best people wouldn't take even a whole kingdom if they had to give up their sense of shame to get it.

edges.reason: Even the wide world isn’t wanted without the fence of shame.
edges.quote: won’t want the wide world unless they have shame as their fence

couplets.gloss: People with a real sense of shame would give up life for it, but would never give it up to stay alive.
couplets.sensitive: praises giving up one's life to escape disgrace

edges.reason: Holds shame dearer than life, which is surrendered sooner than shame is.
edges.quote: They won’t give up shame for life

couplets.gloss: If you don't feel ashamed of what would make others ashamed, virtue itself has reason to be ashamed of you.

edges.reason: Someone unmoved where others feel shame gives righteousness itself reason to feel shame.
edges.quote: righteousness has reason to feel shame

couplets.gloss: Breaking with custom costs you your family's standing, but losing your sense of shame costs you everything good.

edges.reason: Ranks lasting shamelessness above any lapse of principle: it burns all your good.
edges.quote: Shamelessness, once it stays, burns all your good

couplets.gloss: People with no sense of shame aren't really alive: they are like wooden puppets pretending to live.

edges.reason: Without it, a person's living is only an act.
edges.quote: fools you into thinking it is alive

edges.reason: The shameless walk about like puppets, moved but not alive.
edges.quote: move like a wooden puppet

couplets.sensitive: Says people without shame are not really alive.

couplets.gloss: Nothing lifts a family higher than one member's resolve never to stop working for it.

edges.reason: Sets the refusal to rest your hands from the work above everything else.
edges.quote: I won’t rest my hands from the work

edges.reason: Holds up advancing one's family as the thing such labour is for.
edges.quote: Nothing advanceth a man’s family so much

couplets.gloss: Hard work and sound judgment, practised fully and steadily, are what raise a family.

edges.reason: Effort is one of just two things that raise a family.
edges.quote: effort

edges.reason: A clear head has to go with the hard work if a house is to rise.
edges.quote: full understanding

couplets.gloss: When someone commits to lifting up their family, even the gods tuck up their clothes and go ahead of them.

edges.reason: The mere vow to raise your family sends god on ahead.
edges.quote: I will raise my family

couplets.gloss: For those who never let up in raising their family, things work out on their own, even without grand plans.

edges.reason: Unbroken effort for one's family succeeds even with no elaborate plan behind it.
edges.quote: strive without delay for their family

couplets.gloss: Whoever raises their family honestly will find the whole world treating them as one of its own.

edges.reason: A house raised without wrongdoing wins its builder the whole world as kin.
edges.quote: The world gathers round a man who raises his family

couplets.gloss: Being a real man means making the family you were born into great.
keywords: what it means to be a man

edges.reason: Calls being master of the family you were born into the good kind of manliness.
edges.quote: master of the family you were born into

couplets.gloss: As the brave take the worst of a battle, the weight of a family falls on the ones able to carry it.

edges.reason: Ranks those who hold a family up with the brave at the front of a battle.
edges.quote: among your own people too the load falls on those who can carry it

edges.reason: Tells the one who carries everyone that the load came to them because they can bear it.
edges.quote: the load falls on those who can carry it

couplets.gloss: People building up a family get no time off; if they get lazy or too proud, the family goes under.

edges.reason: Taking things easy is named as what brings a house down.
edges.quote: Be idle and think of your pride, and it is ruined

edges.reason: Lifting a family is work with no off season at all.
edges.quote: Those raising a family have no season

couplets.gloss: Must the person who shields their family from every trouble live in a body made for nothing but hardship?

edges.reason: Looks with pity at the worn body of the one who shields a whole family.
edges.quote: only a vessel for suffering

couplets.gloss: A family with no one good to hold it up will collapse when trouble eats away at its base.

edges.reason: Without one good person as its prop, a family falls once trouble reaches its roots.
edges.quote: no good person to stand by and prop it up

couplets.gloss: However far people wander, they still depend on farming for food, so farming, hard as it is, comes first.

edges.reason: For all its toil, ploughing is ranked first among the ways of earning a living.
edges.quote: for all its toil, ploughing comes first

edges.reason: All roaming humanity ends up, in the end, standing behind one implement.
edges.quote: it still follows the plough

couplets.gloss: Farmers hold society together, because they feed everyone who isn't able to do that work.

edges.reason: Every other trade lives on what those who till the land provide.
edges.quote: they carry all who can’t and go off to other work

edges.reason: Speaks of those who plough by name and of the place they hold in the world.
edges.quote: Those who plough are the linchpin of the world

edges.reason: The world is a cart, and those who plough the small pin that keeps it together.
edges.quote: the linchpin of the world

couplets.gloss: Only those who live by farming really live; everyone else eats by depending on someone else.

edges.reason: Calls tilling the one independent living, every other trade being dependence.
edges.quote: All the rest bow to eat

edges.reason: Reserves real life for those who work the ground.
edges.quote: Only those who plough and eat really live

couplets.gloss: People whose fields lie heavy with grain will see other kings' power bow to their own king's.

edges.reason: Ripe grain brings the parasols of many rulers under the farmers’ own.
edges.quote: the shade of ripe grain

couplets.gloss: People who eat what they grow never need to ask anyone, and they give to those who ask without holding back.

edges.reason: Living by your own hands frees you from asking and leaves you able to give.
edges.quote: won’t beg

edges.reason: Describes those who eat by the work of their own hands.
edges.quote: eat by the work of their own hands

couplets.gloss: If farmers stopped working, even people who claim to have given up all desire would be in trouble.

edges.reason: Even those past all wanting cannot do without the crop.
edges.quote: even those who say they have given up all desire can’t stand firm

edges.reason: Everything turns on the hands of those who plough: what happens if they fold them.
edges.quote: If those who plough fold their hands

couplets.gloss: Dry the ploughed earth until it shrinks to a quarter of its weight and the crop will flourish with no manure at all.

edges.reason: Hands down the farmer's craft in figures: dry the soil right and manure can be saved.
edges.quote: the crop will thrive with not a handful of manure

couplets.gloss: Fertilising matters more than ploughing, and once the weeds are out, protecting the crop matters more than watering.

edges.reason: Orders the farmer's tasks: manure above ploughing, and watchful guarding above water.
edges.quote: Manuring profiteth more than the ploughing

couplets.gloss: If the owner stops visiting his land and stays home, it sulks at him like a neglected wife.

edges.reason: Staying put instead of going out to the land is the neglect the land resents.
edges.quote: doesn’t go to it and just stays put

edges.reason: A word to the owner who leaves his fields unvisited.
edges.quote: If the owner doesn’t go to it

edges.reason: Gives the ground a wife’s sulk at being left alone.
edges.quote: sulk like a wife

couplets.gloss: The earth laughs when she sees idle people sit and moan that they've no food.
couplets.sensitive: mocks those who say they have nothing to eat

edges.reason: Laughs at the idle who say they have nothing, since the ground was there to be worked.
edges.quote: sitting idle

edges.reason: Earth becomes a woman amused at those who cry out instead of tilling.
edges.quote: the good woman called earth laughs

couplets.gloss: What is more painful than being poor? Nothing but being poor.

edges.reason: Looks for a worse pain than poverty and can only name poverty again.
edges.quote: Only poverty hurts like poverty

couplets.gloss: Poverty is a wicked thing that takes away your happiness both now and in whatever comes after.

edges.reason: Makes want a villain who robs this world and the next alike.
edges.quote: The sinner called poverty

couplets.gloss: The gnawing need of poverty wears away even inherited refinement and gracious speech.
couplets.sensitive: says poverty strips the poor of dignity

edges.reason: Poverty can destroy even the standing and speech a family has handed down.
edges.quote: destroys, all at once, your old family standing and your fine speech

couplets.gloss: Being poor can push even people from good families into talking in ways that humiliate them.
couplets.sensitive: says want reduces people to grovelling

edges.reason: Not even high birth protects a person from what need does to their speech.
edges.quote: Even in those of good family, poverty brings a weakness

edges.reason: Grovelling words are shown as the humiliation need wrings out of a person.
edges.quote: shameful words

couplets.gloss: The one misfortune of being poor has a thousand smaller miseries hidden inside it.

edges.reason: Opens the one misery called poverty and finds many miseries packed inside.
edges.quote: many miseries come and settle

couplets.gloss: A poor person's words are ignored, even when what they say is true and brilliantly put.
couplets.sensitive: tells the poor their words count for nothing

edges.reason: Even the grandest truth falls flat when the speaker has no money.
edges.quote: the words of the poor lose their meaning

couplets.gloss: Poverty with no virtue to support it can make even your own mother treat you like a stranger.
couplets.sensitive: calls the poor wretches even a mother would disown

edges.reason: Poverty without righteousness can part a man from the very mother who bore him.
edges.quote: even by the mother who bore him

couplets.gloss: Will the poverty that nearly killed me yesterday come back again today?
couplets.sensitive: voices despair at poverty as daily near-death

edges.reason: Gives the poor man's own voice, dreading a new day after yesterday's torment.
edges.quote: the poverty that all but killed me yesterday

couplets.gloss: You could even fall asleep in a fire, but you can't get any rest at all when you are poor.

edges.reason: Sleep, possible even in a blaze, is denied altogether to those in want.
edges.quote: In poverty there is no sleep at all

edges.reason: Makes flames gentler than want: a person can at least sleep among them.
edges.quote: sleep even in the middle of a fire

couplets.gloss: With no means left, the destitute should give up the world entirely; staying in it only eats up other people's salt and gruel.
couplets.sensitive: reads as telling the destitute to give up life

edges.reason: Paints having nothing as a dead end: give up everything, or be the death of salt and gruel.
edges.quote: If those who have nothing don’t give up everything

couplets.gloss: It's fine to ask if you find people who can afford to help; if they pretend they can't, the fault is theirs, not yours.

edges.reason: Allows begging outright, given someone it is right to ask.
edges.quote: If you see someone it is right to beg from, beg

edges.reason: Takes the blame off the asker: a false refusal shames the one who refuses.
edges.quote: the blame is theirs, not yours

couplets.gloss: Even asking for help can be a pleasure, when you get what you need without being made to feel small.

edges.reason: Begging can turn pleasant, so long as what is asked for arrives without pain.
edges.quote: Begging itself is a pleasure

couplets.gloss: There's even some grace in asking from people who know their duty and don't pretend they can't help.

edges.reason: Grants begging a beauty of its own, but only before those with no hiding in their hearts.
edges.quote: There is a beauty even in begging

couplets.gloss: Asking from someone who would never refuse, even while dreaming, is every bit as dignified as giving.

edges.reason: Before such a giver, receiving loses all shame and ranks with giving itself.
edges.quote: Begging is like giving

edges.reason: Praises givers who don’t know how to hide what they have, even in a dream.
edges.quote: those who don’t know how to hide even in a dream

couplets.gloss: People are able to live by asking only because the world has people who do not refuse.

edges.reason: Credits those who never turn the needy away with making such a living possible at all.
edges.quote: there are men in the world that refuse not alms

couplets.gloss: Just seeing people who are free of the meanness of refusing is enough to take away the pain of being poor.

edges.reason: Such givers end the ache of want simply by appearing.
edges.quote: all the misery of poverty ends at once

couplets.gloss: A person in need feels a deep inner gladness on meeting someone who gives without sneering or looking down.

edges.reason: Prizes the gift that comes without scorn or insult.
edges.quote: give without scorn or insult

edges.reason: Looks into the beggar's own heart and finds gladness at such a meeting.
edges.quote: the heart is glad and rejoices deep within

edges.reason: Shows someone being asked how to give: with no sneer, so that the asker's heart lifts.
edges.quote: give without scorn or insult

couplets.gloss: If no one ever asked for help, the world would be as lifeless as puppets going back and forth.

edges.reason: With no one asking there would be no giving, and human life would shrink to a puppet show.
edges.quote: Without people who beg

couplets.gloss: What would generous people have to show for themselves if no one ever came asking?

edges.reason: Gives askers their due: they are what a giver's renown depends on.
edges.quote: if there were none who want to beg and receive

couplets.gloss: Someone asking shouldn't get angry at a refusal: their own need proves another person can be short too.

edges.reason: A direct instruction to the one who asks.
edges.quote: A beggar should not get angry

edges.reason: Forbids bitterness at a refusal: the one who begs must not be angry.
edges.quote: A beggar should not get angry

edges.reason: For anyone turned down: your own shortage shows that the other person may be short too.
edges.quote: The misery of his own poverty is witness enough

couplets.gloss: Never asking at all is worth ten million times more than asking, even from those who give gladly.
couplets.sensitive: ranks those who beg far below those who don't

edges.reason: Even a loving giver does not change the sum: not asking is worth ten million times more.
edges.quote: not begging is worth ten million times more

couplets.gloss: If the Creator meant people to stay alive by begging, let that Creator wander homeless and be destroyed.

edges.reason: Curses the maker of the world to say no one should have to beg to live: the target is the injustice.
edges.quote: let him wander far and perish

couplets.gloss: Nothing is more hard-hearted than telling yourself you will cure your poverty by asking others for money.
couplets.sensitive: calls the decision to beg the hardest of hearts

edges.reason: No hardness is worse than planning to beg your way out of poverty.
edges.quote: I will end the misery of poverty by begging

couplets.gloss: The nobility of someone who won't ask even when they have nothing left is too great for the whole world to contain.
couplets.sensitive: praises refusing help even when destitute

edges.reason: Having nothing at all still can’t make this worth beg, and all the space there is can’t hold it.
edges.quote: the worth that won’t consent to beg

couplets.gloss: Even the thinnest porridge tastes better than anything if you earned it yourself.

edges.reason: Finds watery gruel sweeter than all else once it is one's own earning, owed to no giver.
edges.quote: what your own labour has brought

edges.reason: For someone getting by on very little: what you earn yourself has a taste nothing else has.
edges.quote: Even if it is gruel as thin as water

couplets.gloss: Even if you're only asking for water for a cow, nothing shames the tongue more than asking.
couplets.sensitive: calls any asking deeply humiliating

edges.reason: Puts a request for help at the very bottom of what a tongue can say.
edges.quote: nothing more shaming to the tongue than begging

edges.reason: The dread covers any request at all, even one made for a thirsty cow.
edges.quote: Even if you beg water for a cow

couplets.gloss: I ask just one thing of all who must ask: if you have to, don't go to people who dodge and hide what they have.

edges.reason: Speaks to all who beg, and begs of them in turn.
edges.quote: I beg of everyone who begs

edges.reason: Direct advice for choosing whom to ask: stay away from those who hide what they have.
edges.quote: don’t beg from those who hide what they have

couplets.gloss: Asking is a frail boat that breaks apart the moment it hits the rock of someone's evasion.

edges.reason: One meeting with hiding is enough to wreck it, so unsafe is this way of living.
edges.quote: The unsafe boat called begging

edges.reason: Sends begging out as a boat and makes hiding the rock that splits it.
edges.quote: split apart when it strikes the rock called hiding

couplets.gloss: Thinking about asking makes the heart melt; thinking about being turned away destroys it completely.

edges.reason: Feels the beggar’s lot enough to melt the heart, and the hiding enough to kill it.
edges.quote: The heart melts at the thought of begging

couplets.gloss: A beggar's spirit drains away at a refusal, so where does the refuser's own life hide when saying no?

edges.reason: Measures a rebuff by what it does to the one refused.
edges.quote: At a mere word, the life goes out of those who beg

edges.reason: Wonders how the man who withholds can survive the very no that fells the asker.
edges.quote: Where then does the life of those who hide go to hide?

couplets.gloss: The vile look just like people: I've never seen such a perfect imitation.

edges.reason: Marvels sourly that such creatures can pass so exactly for human.
edges.quote: We have never seen a likeness like it

couplets.gloss: Bad people are luckier than those who know right from wrong, because nothing ever troubles their conscience.

edges.reason: Calls them happier, bitterly, because they have no inner pain to feel.
edges.quote: their hearts have no worries

couplets.gloss: The vile are just like gods, because they too do exactly as they please.

edges.reason: Mock praise: like the gods, they do whatever they please.
edges.quote: like the gods, for they too do whatever they please

couplets.gloss: When a lowlife meets someone equally wicked, he tries to outdo them and feels proud of it.

edges.reason: Meeting a rogue only spurs them to be worse and to boast of it.
edges.quote: they outdo him and swagger

couplets.gloss: Bad people behave only out of fear, and if anything else moves them at all, it's a little greed.

edges.reason: Reduces all their conduct to fear, with a little appetite left over.
edges.quote: Fear is all the good conduct of the low

couplets.gloss: Lowlifes are like a drum: they can't rest until they've broadcast every secret they've been told.

edges.reason: Likens them to a drum, beating out loud whatever was told in trust.
edges.quote: like a drum being beaten

edges.reason: Shows by its opposite the value of guarding what has been entrusted.
edges.quote: they carry the secrets they hear to others and tell them

couplets.gloss: A mean person won't even shake the food off his wet hand for anyone, unless they can smash his jaw.

edges.reason: So grudging that only a fist at the jaw can get a crumb from them.
edges.quote: clenched fists can break their jaws

couplets.gloss: Good people respond to a word; like sugarcane, which must be crushed, the vile only give under force.
couplets.sensitive: says the low must be beaten to yield

edges.reason: Like cane in the press, they yield nothing until force is used on them.
edges.quote: like sugarcane, are of use only when crushed

couplets.gloss: It's enough for a vile person to see someone decently clothed and fed, and he starts digging for their faults.

edges.reason: The mere sight of what others wear and eat sets the low hunting for faults.
edges.quote: they can always find a fault in them

edges.reason: It is another's plain comfort, clothing and food, that sets the fault-finding off.
edges.quote: When the low see what others wear and eat

couplets.gloss: What are lowlifes good for when trouble strikes? Only for selling themselves as fast as they can.

edges.reason: At the first trouble they have just one resource, and it is to put themselves up for sale.
edges.quote: sell themselves, quickly

edges.reason: Selling oneself to escape misfortune is the servile end of a base life.
edges.quote: fit to sell themselves

couplets.gloss: Is she a goddess, a rare peacock, or just a woman in heavy earrings? I'm too bewildered to know.

edges.reason: First sight as pure confusion: he cannot say whether she is a goddess, a peacock or a woman.
edges.quote: My heart is lost in doubt

couplets.gloss: When she looks back at me, it is like a seductive spirit attacking with a whole army behind her.

edges.reason: Her answering look hits him like a goddess with an army at her back.
edges.quote: a goddess who strikes had brought an army with her

couplets.gloss: I'd never known what death was until now: it's a woman with great, fighting eyes.

edges.reason: Only now, at the sight of her, does he learn what dying is.
edges.quote: I never knew before what they call death. Now I know

edges.reason: Death takes a shape at last, and the shape is a woman.
edges.quote: It has a woman’s ways

edges.reason: Her eyes are large, and they fight.
edges.quote: big, battling eyes

couplets.gloss: She seems such an innocent girl, but those warlike eyes consume the life of whoever looks at them.

edges.reason: Simplicity and slaughter together: the blow falls on whoever so much as looks.
edges.quote: eat the life of anyone who sees them

edges.reason: Gives an innocent girl a pair of eyes at war with her.
edges.quote: Her eyes are at odds with this innocent, womanly girl

couplets.gloss: Is that death, or eyes, or a doe's look? This innocent girl's gaze has all three in it.

edges.reason: Cannot decide whether what is looking at him is Death itself.
edges.quote: Is it death?

edges.reason: One glance holds three things at once: death, an eye and a doe.
edges.quote: glance has all three in it

couplets.gloss: Only if her curved eyebrows hid them would her eyes stop making me tremble.

edges.reason: Her eyes go on hurting him unless her own brows shut them away.
edges.quote: her eyes would not cause me this trembling pain

couplets.gloss: The cloth over her breasts is like the cover on a raging elephant's eyes: it holds back something dangerous.

edges.reason: Praises a body so dangerous to look at that it has to be kept covered.
edges.quote: this woman’s firm breasts

edges.reason: Her cloth works like the cover hung over a rutting elephant’s eyes.
edges.quote: the cover over the eyes of a rutting elephant

couplets.gloss: Has my courage, which frightens even enemies who've never met me, been defeated by her lovely forehead?

edges.reason: A warrior whose name shakes his enemies is beaten by a forehead.
edges.quote: has broken before it

couplets.gloss: Why add jewellery to someone with a doe's innocent look and shyness? It only takes away from her.

edges.reason: Finds her charm so complete that other ornaments are no use.
edges.quote: What is the use of decking her with ornaments

edges.reason: Counts her modesty as one of the only two adornments she needs.
edges.quote: the shy look of a doe, and modesty

edges.reason: Takes the jewels away and gives her a look and modesty to wear instead.
edges.quote: ornaments that are strangers to her

couplets.gloss: Liquor pleases only those who drink it; love, unlike it, delights you just by looking.

edges.reason: Desire outdoes drink: it delights at a mere look.
edges.quote: It can’t delight those who merely see, as desire does

edges.reason: Sets liquor, which has to be drunk, against desire, which only has to be seen.
edges.quote: Brewed liquor gives joy only to those who drink it

ideaLinks.reason: Three couplets set them head to head: bending low against self-admiring, free of pride against riding on it, hiding shame against telling faults.
ideaLinks.quote: Greatness always bends low. Smallness admires itself and dresses itself up.

ideaLinks.reason: Loving-kindness is the first of the five pillars that hold up worth.
Take away the readiness to be of use, and one pillar of worth is gone.
Worth leans on a kindly eye towards other people.
The last pillar named under worth is truthfulness.
Loving-kindness is one of the two things that make up courtesy.
Birth in a good family must join loving-kindness before courtesy can appear.
ideaLinks.quote: being born into a good family

ideaLinks.reason: Shame is a pillar of worth in 983, and in 1013 the good that worth is tied to.
Long, unbroken effort is what makes a family grow.
ideaLinks.quote: A family grows through long work

ideaLinks.reason: Sound judgment, joined to effort, is the other thing that raises a house.
Eating by the work of your own hands leaves you able to give to all who beg.
ideaLinks.quote: They give to those who beg, and hide nothing

ideaLinks.reason: Even those who have given up all desire can’t stand firm once those who plough fold their hands.
ideaLinks.quote: even those who say they have given up all desire

ideaLinks.reason: Poverty destroys the old standing and fine speech that a good birth passes down.
ideaLinks.quote: your old family standing and your fine speech

ideaLinks.reason: Need forces grovelling speech even out of the well-born.
ideaLinks.quote: a weakness from which shameful words are born

ideaLinks.reason: People can live by asking only because some never refuse.
ideaLinks.quote: there are people in the world who don’t hide what they have

ideaLinks.reason: Those who would never deny charity end want's pangs by being seen.
ideaLinks.quote: all the misery of poverty ends at once

ideaLinks.reason: The glory of an open hand has nothing to stand on if no one asks.
Sets those moved by a word against those moved only by crushing.
ideaLinks.quote: The worthy are of use at a word. The low, like sugarcane, are of use only when crushed.
